newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian Serbs refuse to accept mail via Sarajevo.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Serbs refuse to accept mail via Sarajevo.

text.p: Bosnian Serbs, seeking to bolster their claims to statehood, are holding up the delivery of some 700,000 letters and parcels destined for Serb-controlled territory, postal officials and western officials said on Tuesday.
Serb nationalist leaders, reluctant to recognise the authority of a single Bosnian state, are refusing to accept the mail which has piled up at Sarajevo's main post office over the past year.

The Serbs have cited security concerns but diplomats say the real reason is that nationalist leaders want to maintain separate communications as one of the ways to keep the country strictly divided along ethnic lines.
Semso Ceric, supervisor of the mail department at the Bosnian Postal, Telephone and Telegraph (PTT) company, said the mail has been pouring in from abroad since February.
"We have a big problem storing it," Ceric told Reuters.
The Serbs have been refusing to accept the mail since February, when NATO peacekeeping troops helped deliver letters that had arrived in Sarajevo.
"The most frequent reason they (Serb authorities) cite is security concerns. They say a letter might explode and a citizen of the Serb republic might get hurt," Ceric said.
But he said concerns about security were groundless because the Bosnian post office conducts thorough checks with x-ray machines to screen mail for any explosives or weapons.
Mail for Bosnia first arrives at collection points in Germany, where authorities there also screen mail for possible explosives, he said.
The Bosnian PTT has offered to allow representatives from the Bosnia's Serb republic to help inspect the mail stacked up in sacks and bundles in the post office warehouse.
Serb authorities have not taken up the offer so far.
Ceric said Russia and some other countries sympathetic to the Bosnian Serbs were violating an international agreement by sending packages to Serb territory through neighbouring Serbia.

Serbia, which has recognised Bosnia as an independent state, was also flouting the agreement and sending the mail to Serbs in Bosnia instead of repecting the Sarajevo PTT as the country's legal postal authority, he said.
"Nobody has the right to prevent a citizen from receiving mail," Ceric said. "A lot of people in the Serb republic may not even be aware they have mail here waiting for them."

Chris Bennett, an analyst with the International Crisis Group, a private agency monitoring the peace process, accused Serb leaders of punishing ordinary people by waging endless battles over political nuances.

"It's very sad that the leaders of Republika Srpska (Serb republic) consider it more important to play around with symbolism than to look after the rights and quality of life of their own citizens," Bennett said.
The Dayton peace agreement obliges the Serbs to recognise a weak central government ruling over a country split into autonomous Serb and Moslem-Croat territories.
Restoring telephone and postal service represents "an essential part of the reconciliation process", said Duncan Bullivant, a spokesman for the international High Representative to Bosnia.

"Any obstruction to that process is not in the spirit of the peace agreement and has to be seen as emanating from a political agenda which doesn't recognise Bosnia as a sovereign state made up of two entities."
